scope: Curated animation catalog focused on narrative works and canonical franchise/studio entries: films, short films, series, TV films, specials, OVAs, ONAs, web series and closely related narrative formats. Franchise/collection integrity and substantial narrative releases take priority over marginal standalone discovery. Music videos, commercials, advertising/promotional/branded campaign assets, functional animation and exhaustive festival-selection mining are outside scope. Festivals and awards may be used only as efficient evidence/discovery sources for otherwise relevant works. Stop a research lane when new source classes no longer produce meaningful catalog value; do not repeat near-identical searches merely because a gap remains.

items.title: Peetrikese unenägu
items.caveat: EFIS identifies this Elbert Tuganov film as the work with which Estonian puppet-film production began; V30 keeps the native title to avoid uncertain English-release naming.

items.title: Metsamuinasjutt
items.genres: Children's, Fairy Tale, Puppet Animation, Nature
items.caveat: The Estonian Film Database Nukufilm collection lists Elbert Tuganov’s 1960 film among the earliest nationally significant puppet-animation works.

items.title: Ott kosmoses
items.genres: Children's, Science Fiction, Adventure, Puppet Animation
items.caveat: EFIS identifies Ott kosmoses as a 1961 Elbert Tuganov puppet film that brought its makers early international recognition.

items.title: Veekandja
items.caveat: EFIS film history identifies Veekandja as Rein Raamat’s 1972 work that established continuous drawn-animation production in Estonia.

items.title: … ja teeb trikke
items.caveat: EFIS database entries catalog the film as 1979, while the database’s historical essay references it as 1978. V30 uses the catalog year 1979 and preserves the discrepancy here.

items.title: Big Tyll

items.title: Kolmnurk

items.title: Hell
items.genres: Dark Fantasy, Experimental, Art Animation, Horror
items.caveat: EFIS catalogs Rein Raamat’s Põrgu as a 1983 animated film bringing Eduard Viiralt’s engravings to life and documents major international festival awards.

items.title: Aeg maha

items.title: Kapsapea

items.title: Saamueli Internet

items.title: Ki-ke-ri-gū!
items.caveat: Filmas.lv identifies Ki-ke-ri-gū! as the first Riga Film Studio puppet-animation film and the beginning of a stable Latvian professional puppet-animation tradition.

items.title: Tīģeris Ņau-Ņau
items.caveat: Filmas.lv catalogs Arnolds Burovs’s 1967 film and notes its early experimentation combining puppets, live action and moving-camera techniques.

items.title: Zelta sietiņš
items.caveat: Filmas.lv presents Roze Stiebra’s 1975 musical short as a key example of Latvia’s early two-dimensional animation tradition.

items.title: Vanadziņš
items.caveat: Filmas.lv identifies Vanadziņš as a 1978 Arnolds Burovs puppet film and the only animation work in the Latvian Cultural Canon.

items.title: Zaķīšu pirtiņa
items.caveat: Filmas.lv describes Roze Stiebra’s 1979 Zaķīšu pirtiņa as one of her most popular and enduring children’s films.

items.title: Kabata
items.caveat: Filmas.lv identifies Kabata (1983) as the film with which Roze Stiebra’s group shifted from cutout/appliqué work to classical drawn animation.

items.title: Vilkas ir siuvėjas
items.caveat: The Lithuanian Film Centre identifies Zenonas Tarakevičius’s 1966 Vilkas ir siuvėjas as the first traditionally drawn animation made in Lithuania.

items.title: Iniciatyva

items.caveat: The Lithuanian Film Centre identifies Iniciatyva (1970) as the first animated film created by the Lithuanian Film Studio and links its allegory to the Prague Spring.

items.title: Medis

items.title: Mįslė

items.caveat: ANIMASYROS 2025’s curated Great Greek Masters program identifies Stamatis Polenakis’s Ntoutse Afigeitai as a 1945 Greek five-minute work; V31 uses that retrospective dating and transliteration.

items.title: Tsouf
items.caveat: ANIMASYROS 2025’s Great Greek Masters retrospective lists Thodoros Maragkos’s Tsouf as a 1969 Greek five-minute animation; V31 keeps the native title without forcing an uncertain English release title.

items.title: I Grammi
items.genres: Social Allegory, Satire, Experimental, Historical Animation
items.caveat: ANIMASYROS 2025 lists I Grammi by Giannis Koutsouris and Nassos Mirmiridis as a 1973 Greek short; V31 adds The Line as the English alias while keeping the transliterated Greek title canonical.

items.title: Kyklos
items.genres: Life Cycle, Allegory, Experimental, Historical Animation
items.caveat: The Thessaloniki Film Festival and ANIMASYROS identify Jordan Ananiadis’s 1981 Greek short The Circle / Kyklos as a distinct landmark in his animation filmography.

items.title: The Hole
items.caveat: The Thessaloniki Film Festival catalogs Jordan Ananiadis’s 1983 Greek animated short The Hole as a satire of social reality; V31 keeps it distinct from later sequels The Hole 2 and The Hole 3.

items.title: Adam (1986)
items.genres: Science Fiction, Post-apocalyptic, Experimental, Adult Animation
items.caveat: The Thessaloniki Film Festival catalogs Jordan Ananiadis’s Adam as a 1986 Greek 12-minute post-nuclear animated work. V31 year-qualifies the canonical title to keep the generic single-word identity unambiguous while retaining Adam as lookup/alias.

items.title: Revnost
items.genres: Satire, Musical Abstraction, Experimental, Historical Animation
items.caveat: CINEMATEK and ACMI catalog Todor Dinov’s Bulgarian 1963 short as Revnost / Jealousy; V31 uses the Bulgarian transliteration as canonical and preserves the English title as alias.

items.title: Yabalkata
items.caveat: CINEMATEK’s Bulgarian animation archive program identifies Yabalkata / La Pomme as a 1963 Todor Dinov and Stoyan Dukov short; V31 also records The Apple as its standard English alias.

items.title: Margaritka
items.caveat: Indiana University Press’s survey of Eastern European cinema identifies The Daisy (Margaritka) as a 1965 Todor Dinov short; Bulgarian National Radio separately identifies it as an emblematic Bulgarian animation work and records its 1967 national children’s-film recognition.

items.title: Zatrudnenie
items.genres: Satire, Social Allegory, Experimental, Historical Animation
items.caveat: CINEMATEK catalogs Ivan Andonov’s 1967 Bulgarian short Zatrudnenie under the English program title Embarrassment; V31 preserves both spellings as one identity.

items.title: Embrio No. M.
items.caveat: Cinematheque of North Macedonia catalogs this 1971 eight-minute animated film; its archive synopsis frames ideology and social machinery as a self-consuming allegory. V32 preserves the historical production state in origin while retaining the present North Macedonian archive lineage.

items.title: Border
items.genres: Political Allegory, Experimental, Satire, Historical Animation
items.caveat: Cinematheque of North Macedonia catalogs Border as a 1976 six-minute animated film and records the Belgrade Golden Medal plus Kekec recognition; its central image is the strengthening of borders through conflict.

items.title: Stop
items.genres: Satire, Caricature, Social Commentary, Historical Animation
items.caveat: The national archive catalogs Stop as a 1976 seven-minute animated film built from 54 international caricaturists and records awards at Belgrade, Oberhausen and Tuzla.

items.title: Three Minutes In Miroslav Bartak
items.caveat: The archive catalogs this as a distinct 1976 four-minute animated film adapting 32 caricatures from Miroslav Bartak’s Skopje exhibition; V32 keeps the archive’s English title verbatim.

items.title: Homo Ekranikus
items.genres: Media Satire, Social Commentary, Experimental, Historical Animation
items.caveat: The individual archive record uses Homo Ekranikus for this 1977 four-minute television-obsession satire and records a Bordighera special award. Some archive chronology material renders the title Homo Ecranicus, retained here as an alias rather than a second identity.

items.title: Five Films Of A Hand
items.genres: Pantomime, Social Satire, Experimental, Historical Animation
items.caveat: The national archive catalogs this as a distinct 1977 four-minute animated film using hand pantomime for five themes including love, corruption, oratory and social problems.

items.title: Adam (5 To 12)
items.caveat: The archive catalogs Adam (5 To 12) as a 1977 six-minute film, explicitly incorporating war archive footage into a countdown-to-destruction allegory, and records the Belgrade Golden Medal for direction.

items.title: Bukvar za pismeni
items.genres: Language, Social Satire, Experimental, Historical Animation
items.caveat: The national archive catalogs Буквар за писмени as a distinct 1978 eleven-minute animated film. V32 uses the Latin transliteration as canonical and retains the archive-history English rendering Primer for the Literate as an alias.

items.title: Otpor
items.genres: Political Allegory, Resilience, Object Animation, Historical Animation
items.caveat: The archive catalogs Отпор as a 1978 seven-minute film and records major prizes at Belgrade, Oberhausen, Annecy and Krakow plus Yugoslav Oscar-candidate status. Official archive material also renders the title Resistance / A Resistance; all are one identity.

items.title: The Last Window
items.caveat: The national archive catalogs The Last Window as a 1979 animated film and records the City of Oberhausen award in 1981. Runtime is not exposed in the current individual English archive record, so V32 does not invent one.

items.title: Circus
items.caveat: The archive catalogs Circus as a distinct 1979 animated film about interpersonal life as circus and records the 1979 Krakow Silver Dragon.

items.title: John Vardar vs the Galaxy
items.caveat: KineNova catalogs the 85-minute 2024 North Macedonia/Hungary/Bulgaria/Croatia feature, records its Sitges world premiere on 5 October 2024 and describes it as the first Macedonian feature animation. Quality remains conservatively calibrated pending broader critical evidence.

items.title: Tolerantia
items.genres: Social Satire, Intolerance, 3D Animation, Adult Animation
items.caveat: Sarajevo Film Festival records Tolerantia as the 2008 Heart of Sarajevo winner for best short and the Sarajevo candidate for the 2008 EFA short-film award; the European Film Academy identifies it as Ivan Ramadan’s first independent short. Tolerance is retained as an English alias.

items.title: The Dragon
items.caveat: The project record identifies original title Aždaja, Bosnia and Herzegovina origin, 12-minute runtime and completion on 16 July 2016. Sarajevo later cataloged the film in its 2017 BiH programme; V32 uses the explicit completion year and preserves the festival-year distinction.

items.title: Birds Like Us
items.origin: Bosnia and Herzegovina / UK / Turkey / US
items.caveat: Sarajevo Film Festival catalogs Birds Like Us / Ptice kao mi as a 2017 84-minute animated first feature from Bosnia and Herzegovina, United Kingdom, Turkey and USA, directed by Faruk Šabanović and Amela Ćuhara. Score remains conservative pending broader critical calibration.

items.title: Mafish Faida
items.caveat: Torino’s film page has a conflicting header year, but its Frenkel biography and filmography explicitly place Mafish Faida in 1936 and identify it as the start of the Mish-Mish Effendi cartoon series. V33 uses 1936 and preserves the spelling variants as aliases.

items.title: Bsant wa Dyasty
items.genres: Comedy, Social Satire, Political Satire, Family
items.caveat: Sayfo documents Bsant wa Dyasty as an Egyptian satirical 3D series that debuted on Nile Life in 2007 and continued with new seasons through 2012. V33 records the series master at its debut year.

items.title: L’Ambouba
items.caveat: Nadia Raïs’s filmmaker page dates L’Ambouba to January 2009 and gives Tunisia / 9 minutes. A parallel portfolio labels production year 2010 and Cinema Tunisien lists 2008–2010 variants; V33 uses the filmmaker’s explicit project date and preserves the discrepancy for later metadata review.

items.title: The Wanted 18
items.genres: Documentary, Political, Historical, Stop Motion, Comedy-Drama
items.caveat: The National Film Board catalogs The Wanted 18 as a 2014 75-minute animated feature by Amer Shomali and Paul Cowan. It combines documentary material with animation/stop-motion; V33 uses the co-production origin reflected in festival records.

items.title: The Princess and the River
items.caveat: ElCinema catalogs the Iraqi animated feature in 1982. Scholarly production histories note that scripting/dubbing were Iraqi while animation production moved to East Germany; V33 therefore preserves both production contexts in origin.

items.title: El Atak
items.caveat: ElCinema catalogs this Iraqi animated series in 2011. Transliteration varies substantially; V33 uses El Atak as the English-facing canonical title and retains Al-ʿAtaak and Arabic title forms as aliases.

items.title: Block 13
items.caveat: Sayfo and broader Middle Eastern animation histories identify Block 13 as a Kuwaiti animated series launched in 2000. Although its visual/comedic debt to South Park is well known, the Kuwaiti program was framed for a general/family audience rather than as an adult-content equivalent.

items.title: Umm Saaf
items.caveat: ElCinema catalogs Umm Saaf as a Kuwaiti animated series first shown in 2008. V33 consolidates apostrophe/transliteration variants at alias level.

items.title: Al-Masageel
items.caveat: AGSI records MBC’s 2011 Al-Masageel as an animated sitcom representing Bedouin history and culture, produced by Amman-based Sketch in Motion; Wamda confirms Jordan-based animation with Saudi voice work. V33 preserves the Saudi/Jordan production context.

items.title: Mohammad al-Fatih
items.caveat: Sayfo’s historical corpus dates Mohammad al-Fatih to 1995 and describes a Saudi-backed production workflow carried out in Turkey. V33 keeps this identity separate from later Turkish works about Mehmed II.

items.title: The Jar: A Tale from the East
items.caveat: The original Syrian production is widely dated 1999, while several international catalog/distribution references list 2001. V33 uses 1999 as the original-film year and preserves 2001 as a distribution/catalogue discrepancy rather than creating a second identity.
items.lookupTitle: The Jar: A Tale from the East
aliases: The Jar: A Tale From the East

items.title: The Jasmine Birds
items.caveat: Sulafa Hijazi’s official portfolio identifies The Jasmine Birds as a 2009 2D feature and the second animated feature produced in Syria, with multiple later international festival awards. Quality remains editorial and unranked pending global calibration.

items.title: Peixonauta
items.caveat: TV PinGuim’s series launched on Discovery Kids in Latin America on 20 April 2009. V34 records the television-series master separately from the already-catalogued 2018 feature film.

items.title: Meu AmigãoZão
items.caveat: The Brazil/Canada coproduction was developed and promoted before launch, creating contradictory secondary metadata that assigns 2008 as an airing year. Apple TV and Brazilian/Latin American launch records converge on 2010; V34 therefore uses 2010 and treats 2008 as development-era metadata rather than a verified series premiere.

items.title: Tromba Trem
items.caveat: The project emerged from AnimaTV and had pilot/development activity in 2010; TV Brasil’s full-series rollout begins in April 2011. V34 uses 2011 for the series master and preserves the earlier AnimaTV roots as context.

items.title: Historietas Assombradas (para Crianças Malcriadas)
items.caveat: Copa Studio dates the television series to 2013 and lists two seasons / 40 episodes. This series master is separate from the already-catalogued feature Haunted Tales for Wicked Kids: The Movie.

items.title: Irmão do Jorel
items.genres: Comedy, Family, Slice of Life, Surrealism
items.caveat: The official Irmão do Jorel site dates the world premiere to 22 September 2014 on Cartoon Network Brazil. V34 records the original series master only.

items.title: O Show da Luna!
items.caveat: The English-language Earth to Luna! rollout began in the United States in August 2014, followed by Discovery Kids Latin America/Brazil in October 2014. V34 uses the shared 2014 series-start year and preserves the transnational first-season production context.

items.title: Osmar, a Primeira Fatia do Pão de Forma
items.caveat: The character/project predates the broadcast series, including a pilot and funding stages. The Gloob television series launched in November 2013; V34 uses 2013 for the series master and does not confuse the earlier pilot/project with a full-series premiere.
items.lookupTitle: Osmar, a Primeira Fatia do Pão de Forma
aliases: Osmar: The Heel of the Loaf

items.title: Tikitiklip
items.caveat: CNTV’s annual documentation states that Tikitiklip was transmitted by TVN from September 2005. V34 keeps the common Tikiticlip spelling as an alias rather than a second identity.

items.title: Diego y Glot
items.genres: Comedy, Family, Slice of Life, Children
items.caveat: CNTV records Diego y Glot as a Chilean children’s animated series transmitted by Canal 13 from September 2005. Later seasons/repeats remain part of this series master.

items.title: Pulentos
items.caveat: CNTV proceedings document the animated series Pulentos in broadcast by November 2005. V34 records the original Chilean series identity and leaves later adaptations/related works separate.

items.title: Block
items.caveat: CNTV documents the Chilean animation Block as broadcast in 2006 and repeated in 2007. Because “Block” is generic, V34 anchors identity to Chile/CNTV/2006; it is not the Kuwaiti Block 13 (2000) already present in V33.

items.title: Zumbástico Fantástico
items.caveat: The anthology block was funded through CNTV in 2008, but broadcast/acquisition records place its Cartoon Network launch in 2011, with TVN following later. V34 uses 2011 as the released series year and preserves 2008 as development/funding context.

items.title: El siguiente programa
items.genres: Adult Comedy, Social Satire, Political Satire
items.caveat: Colombian animation histories place El siguiente programa in 1997 as a domestically produced animated TV series by Conexión Creativa/Gaira/Cenpro. V34 records the original television master; the 2019 short web revival is not a separate master here.

items.title: Betty Toons
items.caveat: RCN Studios identifies Betty Toons as an animated series produced in 2002, built around child versions of the Yo soy Betty, la fea characters. V34 records the series master as a distinct animated spin-off.

items.title: Profesor Súper O
items.caveat: Colombian broadcast references place Profesor Súper O on Canal 13 / Señal Colombia from 2006. V34 consolidates accent and punctuation variants under the same educational-series identity.

items.title: Guillermina y Candelario
items.caveat: Inravisión/Colombian public-media history states that the series first aired regionally on Telepacífico in 2010 and reached national Señal Colombia in 2011. V34 uses the verified first-broadcast year, 2010.

items.title: Cuentos de viejos
items.genres: Animated Documentary, Oral History, Memory, Educational
items.caveat: Development/production of the transmedia project began before broadcast and some catalogues use 2012. Señal Colombia explicitly states that the first season went on air in 2013; V34 therefore uses 2013 as the series premiere year and retains the 2012 project/production start as a caveat.

items.title: Las aventuras de Hijitus
items.caveat: Argentina’s official García Ferré profile states that Hijitus premiered on television in 1967 and was the country’s first animated TV series. V34 records the original microprogram/series master, not later feature compilations.

items.title: Ico, el caballito valiente
items.caveat: Cine Nacional records the film year as 1983 while listing its Argentine theatrical release as 9 July 1987. V34 preserves 1983 as the database year and keeps the 1987 theatrical date explicit rather than silently replacing one with the other.

items.title: Teo, cazador intergaláctico
items.caveat: Cine Nacional records Teo, cazador intergaláctico as a 2004 Argentina/Spain animated coproduction with Argentine commercial release on 9 December 2004.

awards.organization: Academia de las Artes y las Ciencias Cinematográficas de España

items.title: Los Pintín al rescate
items.caveat: Cine Nacional records Los Pintín al rescate as an Argentine animated feature from 2000, released theatrically on 13 July 2000. The film identity is distinct from the short-form television property from which the characters originated.

items.title: Disney's Adventures of the Gummi Bears
items.caveat: D23 records the Disney Television Animation series as premiering on 14 September 1985. V35 adds the television master; shorter English forms are retained only as aliases.
items.lookupTitle: Disney's Adventures of the Gummi Bears

items.title: The Wuzzles
items.caveat: D23 documents the 1985 Disney television series and its 13-episode run. The Disney-branded title form is retained as an alias.

items.title: MoonDreamers
items.caveat: The 15-minute Sunbow/Marvel serial first aired on 25 September 1986 and rotated as a secondary segment within My Little Pony 'n Friends. V35 treats the recurring serial as its own work identity rather than as a duplicate of the parent block.

items.title: Lady Lovely Locks and the Pixietails
items.caveat: The 1987 DIC television adaptation of the American Greetings/Mattel property ran as a single-series master. Common shortened and spacing variants are normalized as aliases.
items.lookupTitle: Lady Lovely Locks and the Pixietails

items.title: Starcom: The U.S. Space Force
items.caveat: The 1987 DIC science-fiction series is retained as a standalone television master distinct from its associated toy line; the production-bible title form supports the identity.

items.title: Sylvanian Families
items.caveat: This record is specifically the 1987 DIC syndicated adaptation of the Epoch toy property, not later Sylvanian Families television adaptations.

items.title: The Glo Friends
items.caveat: The Sunbow/Marvel serial began on 23 September 1986 and rotated as a secondary segment within My Little Pony 'n Friends. V35 records the recurring 26-segment serial as its own identity.

items.title: Bananaman
items.caveat: The UK children’s-television archive records Bananaman as a BBC animated production transmitted from 3 October 1983 to 15 April 1986, with 40 five-minute episodes.

items.title: The World of David the Gnome
items.caveat: Apple TV identifies the BRB Internacional series as a 1985 Spanish production. Spanish and shorter English title forms are preserved as aliases.
items.lookupTitle: The World of David the Gnome

items.title: Seabert
items.caveat: The 1985 French animated series is also known by its original French title Bibifoc; V35 keeps Seabert as the international master title and Bibifoc as an alias.

items.title: The Bluffers
items.caveat: The Dutch-American environmental fantasy series first aired in 1986 and is added as a standalone series master.

items.title: The Adventures of Spot
items.caveat: The King Rollo Films/BBC animated television adaptation began on 9 April 1987. V35 records the series master rather than individual Spot specials.

items.title: Percy the Park Keeper
items.caveat: V35 uses 1996 as the master launch year for the animated Percy the Park Keeper television property, which began with seasonal specials before later short-form episodes.

items.title: The Magic Key
items.caveat: The BBC/Oxford Reading Tree educational animated series first aired on BBC Two on 25 September 2000; the reading-program association is retained as an alias only.
aliases: Oxford Reading Tree: The Magic Key

items.title: Angelina Ballerina
items.caveat: The original HIT Entertainment animated series began on 15 October 2001. It is kept distinct from the later CGI sequel/revival Angelina Ballerina: The Next Steps.

items.title: Angelina Ballerina: The Next Steps
items.caveat: The CGI sequel/revival first aired on 5 September 2009 and is a separate series identity from the 2001 Angelina Ballerina adaptation.

items.title: Jakers! The Adventures of Piggley Winks
items.caveat: The CGI children’s series began on 7 September 2003 and ran for 52 episodes. V35 preserves Jakers! as a shortened alias while keeping the full master title.
items.lookupTitle: Jakers! The Adventures of Piggley Winks

items.title: Corduroy
items.caveat: This record is the 2000 Nelvana animated television series, distinct from the earlier direct-to-video adaptation of Don Freeman’s character.

items.title: The Berenstain Bears (1985)
items.caveat: The explicit year suffix prevents collision with the separate 2002 animated adaptation. The contemporary The Berenstain Bears Show title is preserved as an alias.

items.title: The Berenstain Bears (2002)
items.caveat: The explicit year suffix distinguishes the Nelvana-produced 2002 television adaptation from the 1985 series. V35 intentionally does not assign the unqualified title as an alias.

items.title: The Adventures of Paddington Bear
items.caveat: The 1997 CINAR/Protecrea animated series is distinct from the 1976 FilmFair adaptation and later Paddington television incarnations; no unqualified Paddington Bear alias is used.

items.title: Special Agent Oso
items.caveat: D23 records the Walt Disney Television Animation series as premiering on 4 April 2009. V35 uses the broadcast year rather than development-era 2008 metadata found on some Disney pages.

items.title: Mike the Knight
items.caveat: The Nelvana/HIT preschool series premiered in Canada in 2011 and is added as the television-series master.

items.title: Tree Fu Tom
items.caveat: BBC programme records document Tree Fu Tom on CBeebies in 2012; V35 adds the CGI/live-participation preschool animation master.

items.title: Poko
items.caveat: The Canadian stop-motion preschool series began on CBC Television on 9 June 2003 and ran for 52 episodes.

items.title: El maná
items.caveat: Jesús de Armas recalled that El maná was made in 1959 but first exhibited in 1960 after laboratory processing delays; V36 uses the public-release year and treats it as the first ICAIC animated short.

items.title: La prensa seria
items.caveat: Jesús de Armas places production in 1959 and exhibition in 1960; some later histories list 1961. V36 uses 1960 and preserves the date discrepancy rather than silently normalizing it.

items.title: El profesor Bluff
items.caveat: The dedicated restoration/research page catalogs Tulio Raggi’s film as 1964; a longer critical essay discusses it as a 1963 work. V36 uses 1964 as the catalog/release year and preserves the 1963 dating as a caveat.

items.title: Macrotí, un Noé cubano
items.caveat: Cuban film historiography commonly catalogs the short in 1965, while research notes that physical completion dates to 1963. V36 uses the established catalog year and preserves the earlier completion date.

items.title: Una aventura de Elpidio Valdés
items.caveat: Spain’s ICAA catalog records 1974 as the production year; its later 1984 Spanish certification/release is distribution metadata, not the work’s identity year.

items.title: El enanito sucio
items.caveat: Cinemateca Portuguesa catalogs Juan Padrón’s Cuban short as a 1975 ICAIC production and preserves it in its deposited Cuba-animation program.

items.title: Elpidio Valdés contra la policía de Nueva York
items.caveat: Ibermedia’s Juan Padrón biofilmography lists the 1976 short as a distinct Elpidio Valdés work; V36 retains the Spanish original title as canonical.
items.lookupTitle: Elpidio Valdés contra la policía de Nueva York
aliases: Elpidio Valdes contra la policia de Nueva York

items.title: Elpidio Valdés encuentra a Palmiche
items.caveat: Ibermedia and Cuban archival filmographies consistently identify this Palmiche-centered Elpidio Valdés short as a distinct 1977 work.

items.title: Elpidio Valdés contra la cañonera
items.caveat: Ibermedia’s Padrón filmography lists the short separately in 1980, distinguishing it from the 1979 and 1983 Elpidio Valdés feature films already in the catalog.

items.title: Filminuto 1
items.caveat: Filminutos documentation identifies the 1980 work as the opening compilation in ICAIC’s long-running one-minute animated-comedy cycle; Cinemateca Portuguesa describes it as four micro-shorts.

items.title: ¡Viva papi!
items.caveat: Ibermedia’s Juan Padrón biofilmography dates the short to 1982; it later received a Caracol animation award in Cuba.

items.title: El bohío
items.caveat: ENDAC’s work-specific entry dates Mario Rivas’s ICAIC short to 1984. Some later secondary summaries use 1985 or 1986; V36 follows the dedicated archive-style record and preserves the discrepancy.

items.title: Quinoscopio 1
items.caveat: ENDAC and Ibermedia filmographies list Quinoscopio 1 in 1985, while ENDAC narrative biography text says the first Quinoscopio appeared in 1986. V36 uses the filmography year and preserves the alternate dating.

items.title: El pequeño planeta perdido
items.caveat: ENDAC’s Mario García-Montes filmography dates the short to 1990 and records multiple awards, including a New York Latino festival animation prize and Cuban critics’ recognition.

items.title: Pacto Andino
items.caveat: COPROCI technical records date Rafael Seminario’s animated short to 5 May 1976; the 2026 Ministry of Culture restoration program independently lists it as 1976.

items.title: Facundo
items.caveat: COPROCI records date Fernando Gagliuffi’s short to 14 September 1976. The 2026 national restoration program likewise catalogs Facundo as 1976.

items.title: El mito de Inkarri
items.caveat: COPROCI records date Mario Acha Kutscher’s animated treatment of Guaman Poma imagery and the Inkarri myth to 1 March 1977. The 2026 restoration program spells the title “El mito de Inkari”; V37 keeps the technical-record spelling and stores the modern variant as an alias.

items.title: El cóndor y el zorro
items.caveat: COPROCI records date Walter Tournier’s Peruvian Caracol Producciones short to 5 June 1980. Historical accounts identify it as the first Peruvian short to win the Coral animation prize at Havana.

items.title: El chicle
items.caveat: COPROCI records date Nelson García Miranda’s mixed live-action/plasticine-animation short to 15 February 1982. The 2026 Ministry of Culture restoration program independently catalogs it as 1982.

items.title: Un país sin desarrollo
items.caveat: The COPROCI technical record gives 10 November 1983 and identifies the film as an animated public-information short encouraging tax payment. A 2026 Ministry of Culture restoration program labels the same work 1989; V37 uses the dated exhibition certificate while preserving that later archival discrepancy.

items.title: La misma vaina
items.caveat: The COPROCI certificate is dated 6 December 1984. Rivera’s narrative history describes the Facundo follow-up as having premiered in Lima in 1983; V37 uses the dated exhibition certificate and preserves the earlier premiere claim as a caveat.

items.title: La oscuridad colorida
items.caveat: COPROCI records date Víctor Sarmiento Castro’s film to 12 September 1985, matching the 2026 Ministry of Culture restoration program. Earlier narrative summaries sometimes use 1983; V37 follows the exhibition certificate/restoration year.

items.title: El perfil de lo invisible
items.caveat: The COPROCI certificate is dated 29 January 1987. The 2026 Ministry of Culture restoration program labels the work “1974/1987”, reflecting its unusually long gestation, while Rivera’s narrative history also associates completion/award activity with 1986. V37 uses the exhibition-certificate year and preserves all three chronology signals.

items.title: Animatógrafo
items.caveat: COPROCI records date Benicio Vicente Kou’s 10-minute Antarki film to 8 November 1989. The short teaches pre-cinema optical devices and animation technique and also presents the Cuniraya myth.

items.title: Al toque de queda
items.caveat: COPROCI records date Roberto Bonilla and Javier Prado’s eight-minute short to 14 June 1990. The 2026 Ministry of Culture restoration program also catalogs it as 1990; its premise follows a character’s misadventures during Lima’s curfew.

items.title: El clavel desobediente
items.caveat: Rivera documents Walter Tournier’s 1981 11-minute short as a mixed puppetry/animation adaptation of a Jorge Díaz Herrera poem, produced with major participation from the Kusi Kusi puppet group. The film’s freedom-and-nurture theme is work-specific and well documented.

items.title: Ir por lana
items.caveat: Rivera’s production history dates Javier Prado’s cel-animated 35 mm short to 1983 and credits Prado with script and animation. Prado’s later recollections give 1987, while an older event listing used 1988; V38 follows the scholarly 1983 chronology and preserves the conflict instead of silently normalizing it.

items.title: Nuestro pequeño paraíso
items.caveat: Rivera documents Walter Tournier’s nine-minute 1983 plasticine short as his screenwriting debut: a satire about an individual alienated by television. Period criticism singled it out as one of Tournier’s strongest works from his Peruvian period, supporting an above-average historical assessment.

items.title: Cuniraya Viracocha
items.caveat: Antarki completed this two-minute 1984 CETUC-PUCP co-produced pilot after the concept evolved from a proposed feature into a proposed television series. The larger project was never produced; V38 records only the completed pilot, which Rivera describes as surviving evidence of a high-artistic-level team effort.

items.title: El fabuloso mundo de la fábula
items.caveat: Rivera’s illustrated history captions El fabuloso mundo de la fábula as a Benicio Vicente 1986 production and describes La Fábula as a set of animated shorts planned for television. V38 treats the extant 1986 production as one work-level short/anthology master and does not invent an unrealized series master.
items.lookupTitle: El fabuloso mundo de la fábula

items.title: Fuego
items.caveat: Rivera attributes the 1988 short Fuego to Máximo Geldres, while contemporary Peruvian criticism discusses Carlos Elorriaga as its realizing filmmaker and describes a volcanic-explosion visual gag. The work identity and year are stable; the creator-credit discrepancy is preserved for later archival resolution.

items.title: Pedro Paulet Mostajo
items.caveat: Rivera’s illustrated history identifies Pedro Paulet Mostajo as a 1989 animated short by Augusto Cabada and Carlos Valle. Later creator recollections also place Pedro Paulet within the Chimu Films production cycle. V38 uses the full documented title to avoid confusion with unrelated biographies of the Peruvian scientist.

items.title: Navidad Caribeña
items.genres: Comedy, Family, Political Satire, Stop Motion, Christmas
items.caveat: The RECAM/Uruguay Film Commission catalogue records Walter Tournier’s 24-minute film in 2001 and documents its extensive festival recognition. Production was Welsh-Uruguayan (including S4C); V38 therefore uses Uruguay / UK rather than flattening the coproduction to a single-country master.

items.title: Tachuela, Varilla y Lechuga
items.caveat: Tournier filmography materials document this four-minute 2D short in 2003: three characters fail while working separately and succeed through cooperation. Divercine prizes support a solid work-level assessment.

items.title: La canilla perfecta
items.caveat: The Animadrid 2008 programme lists Walter Tournier’s Uruguayan The Perfect Faucet / La canilla perfecta, while Tournier filmography describes a 7½-minute main stop-motion film accompanied by four short water-care spots. V38 records the principal short as one master and does not split the related spots into redundant entries.

items.title: La cama
items.genres: Surreal Comedy, Object Animation, Stop Motion
items.caveat: Uruguay’s Ministry of Education and Culture programme gives 2008 as the production year for Walter Tournier’s one-minute La cama; several later filmographies list 2009. V38 follows the government production year and preserves the alternate 2009 dating as a chronology caveat.

items.title: Chatarra
items.caveat: Uruguay’s national-cinema programme records Walter Tournier’s five-minute Chatarra as a 2015 animation and summarizes it as memories of life in an apocalyptic world. V38 uses the national-programme year and a work-specific dark/disturbing profile.

items.title: Alto el juego
items.caveat: The FICDH programme identifies Alto el juego / Cease Game as a silent seven-minute Uruguayan animation from 2016 by Walter Tournier, following a child and dog trying to shelter amid war. The severe violence/disturbing profile reflects the film’s bombardment, death and displacement context rather than graphic gore.

items.title: La danza de los esqueletos
items.caveat: Academic research identifies Herbert Weisz’s 1934 Laboratorios Nacionales short as the foundational Venezuelan animation milestone and links it to the country’s early sound-technology experiments. Surviving descriptions also preserve period caricatures of Indigenous people; V39 flags that historical stereotype context rather than modernizing the work description.

items.title: Conejín
items.caveat: The Fundación Cinemateca Nacional retrospective identifies José “Castillito” Castillo’s Conejín as a 1975 Venezuelan short and the starting point for his recurring rabbit character. The hand-made direct-on-film practice is central to Castillo’s historical importance, but V39 does not split later Conejín appearances into separate franchise objects without work-level titles.

items.title: El cuatro de hojalata
items.genres: Children's, Animals, Stop Motion, Social Allegory
items.caveat: A Focus Venezuela festival dossier identifies Alberto Monteagudo’s El cuatro de hojalata as a 1978, 13-minute Venezuelan animation; period festival records also document its Coral recognition. Fundación Empresas Polar gives 1976, so V39 retains 1978 as the canonical work year while explicitly preserving the alternate chronology.

items.title: Manzanita
items.genres: Children's, Literary Adaptation, Stop Motion, Fantasy
items.caveat: The Universidad de Los Andes historical archive records Armando Arce’s animated adaptation of Julio Garmendia as a 1978 production. Other secondary histories circulate 1970 or 1979 dates; V39 follows the ULA production record and preserves those alternatives as chronology conflicts rather than duplicate masters.

items.title: Wanadi
items.genres: Indigenous Mythology, Folklore, Stop Motion, Fantasy
items.caveat: Academic Venezuelan filmography lists Armando Arce’s Wanadí as a 1981 animated short (35 mm, about 17 minutes) based in Indigenous mythic material. Some later biographical summaries shift the date to 1983; V39 follows the academic filmography and stores the accented spelling as an alias.

items.title: La cueva
items.caveat: The Fundación Cinemateca Nacional retrospective dates José Castillo’s three-minute La cueva to 1985, follows Conejín inside Cueva del Guácharo, and records a Hans Christian Andersen award at the Odense festival. V39 treats it as its own work-level short rather than a Conejín episode object.

items.title: La cucarachita
items.caveat: The Fundación Cinemateca Nacional retrospective dates José Castillo’s adaptation of the Venezuelan children’s tale La cucarachita Martínez to 1987. V39 uses the shorter film title as canonical and keeps the tale title as an alias.

items.title: Kimono
items.caveat: The Fundación Cinemateca Nacional retrospective dates José Castillo’s Kimono to 1992 and describes it as an animation based on Pascual Venegas Filardo’s poem La niña del Japón, presenting nineteenth-century Japanese life. The generic title is gated by the 1992 Venezuela/Castillo identity tuple.

items.title: La princesa y el guisante
items.genres: Children's, Fairy Tale, Literary Adaptation, Experimental
items.caveat: The Fundación Cinemateca Nacional retrospective dates José Castillo’s one-minute version of the Hans Christian Andersen tale to 1993. V39 records the compact standalone short and does not infer additional adaptation material beyond the documented work.

items.title: Safari
items.caveat: The Fundación Cinemateca Nacional retrospective dates José Castillo’s two-minute Safari to 1995 and identifies it as a Conejín visit to Safari Carabobo. A CNAC-derived secondary list gives 1991; V39 uses the Cinemateca year and protects the highly generic title with the Venezuela/Castillo identity tuple.

items.title: Fiesta
items.caveat: The Fundación Cinemateca Nacional retrospective dates José Castillo’s Fiesta to 2001 and describes Venezuelan Cruz de Mayo and coastal/llanos popular festivities. A scholarly essay gives 1987; V39 follows the national retrospective and protects this generic title with the 2001 Venezuela/Castillo identity tuple.

items.title: Temerario
items.caveat: Visor lists Temerario under 2006 Venezuelan animation, credited to Carl Zitelmann. Because the title is generic and public work-level detail is sparse, V40 uses creator/year/origin disambiguation and does not infer narrative content.

items.title: El Pianógrafo
items.caveat: Museo Reina Sofía’s Vaivén programme lists Eduardo Brenes’s El Pianógrafo as Costa Rica/2008. V41 keeps the accented canonical title and an ASCII alias for provider matching.

items.title: ANNA
items.caveat: Costa Rica’s national film-centre winners register lists ANNA by Sequeira/Guillén/Porras (Studios Flex) as Best Animation in the 2005 Muestra. The all-caps generic title is guarded by creator/studio/year context; public synopsis evidence remains sparse.

items.title: Animales de alquiler
items.genres: Science Fiction, Dystopian, Environmental, Stop Motion
items.caveat: Costa Rica’s national winners register names Pablo Ortega’s Animales de alquiler as Best Animation in 2010. Contemporary festival documentation describes a stop-motion future where rainforest species are extinct and people host animal genetic material in exchange for aid.

items.title: Adán y Eva en el Paraíso de Judith Gutiérrez
items.caveat: Ecuador’s Archivo AANM documents Paco Cuesta’s 1982 frame-by-frame cine-installation/short, based on Judith Gutiérrez’s paintings, at about eight minutes. Other retrospective sources report roughly 6:30–7:30 after deterioration/transfer; V41 keeps one 1982 master and preserves the runtime/condition discrepancy.

items.title: Afterwork
items.caveat: Annecy’s archive lists Afterwork as a 2017 Ecuador/Spain/Peru 3D short by Luis Usón and Andrés Aguilar (6:12), aimed at adults/young adults and centered on repetitive work routines. One master covers the multinational production.

items.title: Testigo del Viento
items.caveat: Premios Colibrí lists Fernanda Caicedo’s Testigo del Viento as an Ecuadorian 2022 seven-minute stop-motion work produced at Bauhaus University; German festival/foundation sources describe it as a Germany–Ecuador coproduction. V41 stores Ecuador / Germany and preserves the national-catalogue wording in this caveat.

items.title: Papiroflexia
items.caveat: Paraguay’s Secretaría Nacional de Cultura repeatedly programs Joaquín Baldwin’s Papiroflexia as national animation; international records date it to 2007 and note U.S. school-production context. V41 therefore uses Paraguay / US instead of flattening either attribution.

items.title: Sebastian's Voodoo
items.caveat: Paraguay’s Secretaría Nacional de Cultura treats Joaquín Baldwin’s film as local/national animation, while its 2008 UCLA Animation Workshop production and U.S. release are independently documented. V41 stores Paraguay / US and keeps one 2008 master.

items.title: The Windmill Farmer
items.caveat: Paraguay’s Secretaría Nacional de Cultura includes The Windmill Farmer among national animation and elsewhere labels it PY–US. The 2010 UCLA production context is also documented. V41 therefore uses Paraguay / US and one work-level master.

items.title: Oscuro Cardinal
items.caveat: UNAH’s critical history records Adrián Guerra’s Oscuro Cardinal as a 2008 Honduran animation, while contemporary Ícaro coverage confirms its national animation-category presence. Scholarship describes its child/war allegory; V41 keeps one 2008 master.

items.title: Víctimas de Guernica
items.caveat: Production documentation identifies Ferrán Caum’s 2015 clay stop-motion short as an El Salvador / Spain work linking Picasso’s Guernica with civilian victims of El Salvador’s civil war. Spain’s ICAA treats the registered production as Spanish; V41 preserves the Salvadoran realization context rather than flattening it.

steps.title: El-Hazard: The Wanderers
steps.note: 26-episode television retelling/alternate continuity.

franchises.name: Patlabor
franchises.summary: Branch-aware guide separating the original Early Days/film continuity, the television/New Files continuity and the new Patlabor EZY line.

steps.title: WXIII: Patlabor the Movie 3
steps.note: Later-produced film-side story; chronologically set roughly between the first two films but best treated as an optional theatrical branch.

franchises.name: Space Battleship Yamato
franchises.summary: Branch-aware Yamato route: the 1978 theatrical ending and Yamato 2 continuity diverge, while 2199/2202/2205/3199 form the modern remake line. Recap/compilation films are intentionally omitted.

steps.title: Space Battleship Yamato: The New Voyage

orders.label: Classic alternate theatrical ending

franchises.name: Captain Harlock
franchises.summary: Harlock has several incompatible screen continuities. The original TV series, Arcadia/SSX line, Harlock Saga, Endless Odyssey revival and 2013 CGI reboot are kept as separate branches.

steps.title: Arcadia of My Youth: Endless Orbit SSX
Harlock Saga
steps.note: Standalone alternate Leijiverse adaptation.

steps.title: Space Pirate Captain Herlock: The Endless Odyssey
steps.note: Later revival of the classic Harlock setup; not a continuation of Harlock Saga.

franchises.name: Galaxy Express 999
franchises.summary: Core screen route only: the long TV adaptation is independent from the theatrical feature sequence. Minor specials and broader Leijiverse crossovers are intentionally omitted.

franchises.name: Space Cobra / Cobra
franchises.summary: The 1982 film and television series are alternate classic adaptations; the 2008–10 Cobra the Animation releases form a later revival sequence.

franchises.name: Cowboy Bebop
franchises.summary: Compact complete screen route. The movie is set during the television story but is easiest to watch after the series.

franchises.name: Armitage III
franchises.summary: The four-part OVA is the story-bearing first entry; Poly-Matrix is a re-edit variant and therefore not a separate step. Dual-Matrix is the distinct sequel.

franchises.name: Dominion Tank Police
franchises.summary: Three screen interpretations of Masamune Shirow’s Dominion/Tank Police material. Tank S.W.A.T. 01 is a later CG reinterpretation, not a required direct sequel.

franchises.name: Vampire Hunter D
franchises.summary: Two standalone feature-length adaptations from the novel series rather than one serialized screen continuity.

franchises.name: Ninja Scroll
franchises.summary: The television series follows the feature’s Jubei screen incarnation and is placed after the film for a compact release-order route.

franchises.name: Record of Lodoss War
franchises.summary: The 1990 OVA and 1998 television series overlap in source material and should be treated as alternate adaptation routes rather than one continuous season chain.

steps.title: Record of Lodoss War: Chronicles of the Heroic Knight

franchises.name: Black Jack
franchises.summary: Separate classic OVA/film and 2004 TV-era branches, plus Young Black Jack as a later prequel/reimagining. Minor web/special shorts are outside this integrity pass.

steps.title: Black Jack: The Two Doctors of Darkness

franchises.name: Space Runaway Ideon
franchises.summary: The 1980 television series and Be Invoked form the story-bearing core. A Contact is an edited TV compilation with some new cuts and is intentionally not a separate catalog master.

steps.title: The Ideon: Be Invoked
steps.note: Concluding film containing the previously unseen ending.

franchises.name: Hunter x Hunter
franchises.summary: Two separate anime adaptations. The 1999 television continuity continues through three OVAs; the 2011 series is a full reboot. The 2013 films are optional standalone branches tied to the modern cast/era.

steps.title: Hunter x Hunter: The Last Mission

franchises.name: Gintama
franchises.summary: The catalog keeps the television run under one series master. The 2010 Benizakura theatrical retelling is intentionally excluded as repackage material; the original-story 2013 film and the 2021 bridge/finale remain distinct narrative works.

steps.title: Gintama: The Movie: The Final Chapter: Be Forever Yorozuya
steps.note: Original-story feature, not required for the final TV-to-film conclusion.

franchises.name: The King of Braves GaoGaiGar
franchises.summary: The 1997 television series continues directly into the eight-episode FINAL OVA. The later Grand Glorious Gathering television version is a re-edited presentation of FINAL and is not duplicated as a master.

steps.title: The King of Braves GaoGaiGar FINAL

franchises.name: Sound! Euphonium
franchises.summary: The television seasons remain one series master. New-story theatrical/special material is kept separately; compilation films are omitted as duplicate narrative packaging.

steps.title: Sound! Euphonium: The Movie - Our Promise: A Brand New Day
